claim: The GeneWeld knock-in cassette was targeted to exon 2 of the mitfa gene, which leads to disruption of the endogenous mitfa gene.
source: The knock-in cassette, containing Cas9 and BFP driven by the eye-specific γ-crystallin promoter, was targeted to exon 2 of the mitfa gene, which leads to disruption of the endogenous mitfa gene (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript directly states that targeting the knock-in cassette to exon 2 leads to disruption of the endogenous mitfa gene.

claim: Exon 2 is the sole exon shared among the three mitfa protein-coding transcripts.
source: First, this is the sole exon shared among the three mitfa protein-coding transcripts.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this fact about the mitfa gene structure.

claim: An average of 19% of injected embryos had detectable ocular BFP expression at 3 days post-fertilization (dpf), indicating successful integration.
source: An average of 19% of injected embryos had detectable ocular BFP expression at 3 days post-fertilization (dpf), indicating successful integration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from experiments showing BFP expression as a marker of integration.

claim: Precise integration of the knock-in cassette at the mitfa locus was detected in all four sequenced F1 fish.
source: We sequenced four F1 fish and detected on-target integration at the mitfa locus in all four fish (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports sequencing results confirming on-target integration in all tested fish.

claim: One copy of mitfa is sufficient for the normal development of neural crest-derived melanocytes in zebrafish.
source: In zebrafish, one copy of mitfa is sufficient for the normal development of neural crest-derived melanocytes, but loss of both copies of mitfa results in loss of the melanocyte lineage (White et al., 2008; Lister et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work to support this claim.

claim: Loss of both copies of mitfa results in loss of the melanocyte lineage in zebrafish.
source: In zebrafish, one copy of mitfa is sufficient for the normal development of neural crest-derived melanocytes, but loss of both copies of mitfa results in loss of the melanocyte lineage (White et al., 2008; Lister et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work to support this claim.

claim: WT and mitfaCas9 fish exhibited indistinguishable melanocyte patterning during both embryonic and adult stages.
source: WT and mitfaCas9 fish exhibited indistinguishable melanocyte patterning during both embryonic and adult stages.
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data comparing WT and mitfaCas9 fish.

claim: Fish carrying two copies of Cas9 (mitfaCas9/Cas9) resembled the nacre mutant (mitfa-/-), characterized by complete loss of melanocytes.
source: However, as expected, fish carrying two copies of Cas9 (mitfaCas9/Cas9) resembled the nacre mutant (mitfa-/-), characterized by complete loss of melanocytes, indicating the endogenous mitfa gene is disrupted on knock-in alleles (Lister et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data and cites prior work on the nacre mutant.

claim: Cas9 expression was observed in an average of 86% of mitfa+ cells in mitfaCas9 embryos.
source: In mitfaCas9 embryos, Cas9 expression was observed in an average of 86% of these mitfa+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from FISH experiments.

claim: Large-scale GWASs have repeatedly identified SNPs in slc45a2 as tightly linked to human skin color variation.
source: Large-scale GWASs have repeatedly identified SNPs in this gene as tightly linked to human skin color variation, and germline disruption leads to a complete loss of pigmentation in melanocytes (Fernandez et al., 2008; Branicki et al., 2008; Streisinger et al., 1986).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published GWAS studies.

claim: Germline disruption of slc45a2 leads to a complete loss of pigmentation in melanocytes.
source: Large-scale GWASs have repeatedly identified SNPs in this gene as tightly linked to human skin color variation, and germline disruption leads to a complete loss of pigmentation in melanocytes (Fernandez et al., 2008; Branicki et al., 2008; Streisinger et al., 1986).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on slc45a2 function.

claim: 92% of F0 MG-albino fish had mosaic loss of pigmentation within the melanocyte stripe regions.
source: Upon adulthood, 92% of F0 MG-albino fish had mosaic loss of pigmentation within the melanocyte stripe regions (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from experiments with MG-albino fish.

claim: Unpigmented regions in MG-albino fish maintained GFP expression.
source: Unpigmented regions maintained GFP expression (Figure 2B), indicating that the breaks in melanocyte stripes arise from loss of pigmentation in melanocytes rather than loss of the melanocyte lineage (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data from fluorescence imaging.

claim: The breaks in melanocyte stripes in MG-albino fish arise from loss of pigmentation in melanocytes rather than loss of the melanocyte lineage.
source: Unpigmented regions maintained GFP expression (Figure 2B), indicating that the breaks in melanocyte stripes arise from loss of pigmentation in melanocytes rather than loss of the melanocyte lineage (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from the observation that GFP expression is maintained in unpigmented regions.

claim: F1 MG-albino fish exhibited a near-complete loss of pigmentation.
source: F1 MG-albino fish exhibited a near-complete loss of pigmentation, demonstrating that our mitfaCas9 system is highly efficient in F1 fish (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: The manuscript reports observational and quantitative data from F1 fish.

claim: A measurable pigmentation loss in F2 MG-albino melanocytes was observed as early as 3 dpf.
source: Imaging revealed a measurable pigmentation loss in F2 MG-albino melanocytes as early as 3 dpf (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative imaging data from F2 embryos.

claim: F2 MG-albino fish maintained loss of pigmentation throughout development.
source: F2 MG-albino fish maintained loss of pigmentation throughout development, indicating the sustained activity of mitfaCas9 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data from developmental time course experiments.

claim: Robust inactivation of the albino gene was observed in GFP+ (mitfa-expressing) cells.
source: Despite this, robust inactivation of the albino gene was observed in GFP+ (mitfa-expressing) cells, confirming somatic inactivation (Figure 2I).
evidence: The manuscript reports CRISPR-seq data showing indels in GFP+ cells.

claim: The majority of indels in the albino gene were frameshift-inducing mutations.
source: The majority of indels were frameshift-inducing mutations.
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of CRISPR-seq data.

claim: sox10 is a transcription factor vital to the neural crest lineage and indispensable for overall survival of both zebrafish and mice.
source: To assess the effectiveness of our mitfaCas9 model in detecting negative phenotypes, we utilized it to target sox10, a transcription factor vital to the neural crest lineage and indispensable for overall survival of both zebrafish and mice (Dutton et al., 2001; Hou et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on sox10 function.

claim: Germline knockout of sox10 in zebrafish leads to severe defects in peripheral nerve development and the complete absence of melanocytes.
source: Germline knockout of sox10 in zebrafish leads to severe defects in peripheral nerve development and the complete absence of melanocytes, and the animals die around day 14 (Dutton et al., 2001; Kelsh et al., 1996; Carney et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on sox10 germline knockout phenotypes.

claim: sox10-/- zebrafish die around day 14.
source: Germline knockout of sox10 in zebrafish leads to severe defects in peripheral nerve development and the complete absence of melanocytes, and the animals die around day 14 (Dutton et al., 2001; Kelsh et al., 1996; Carney et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on sox10 germline knockout phenotypes.

claim: mitfaCas9 fish injected with an MG-sox10 plasmid exhibited noticeable gaps in their melanocyte stripes.
source: mitfaCas9 fish injected with an MG-sox10 plasmid exhibited noticeable gaps in their melanocyte stripes (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data from F0 fish.

claim: Germline deletion of a sox10 enhancer region affects adult stripe patterning in zebrafish.
source: Germline deletion of a sox10 enhancer region similarly affects adult stripe patterning in zebrafish (Cunningham et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on sox10 enhancer deletion.

claim: The gaps in the stripes of sox10 F0 fish were not occupied by unpigmented GFP+ melanocytes.
source: In contrast to the albino F0 fish, the gaps in the stripes of the sox10 F0 fish were not occupied by unpigmented GFP+ melanocytes, indicating a potential defect in the survival or differentiation of melanocytes upon loss of sox10.
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data comparing sox10 and albino F0 fish.

claim: Loss of sox10 in melanocytes indicates a potential defect in the survival or differentiation of melanocytes.
source: In contrast to the albino F0 fish, the gaps in the stripes of the sox10 F0 fish were not occupied by unpigmented GFP+ melanocytes, indicating a potential defect in the survival or differentiation of melanocytes upon loss of sox10.
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from the observation that gaps lack GFP+ cells.

claim: MG-sox10 F1 fish showed an apparent widening of the interstripe region and narrowing of the melanocyte stripes.
source: However, the opposite is true for MG-sox10 F1 fish, where we observed an apparent widening of the interstripe region and narrowing of the melanocyte stripes (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements of stripe and interstripe widths.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the number of melanocytes in F1 sox10 KO fish compared to F1 NT fish.
source: Melanocytes were counted in fish treated with epinephrine to aggregate melanosomes, revealing a significant reduction in the number of melanocytes in the F1 sox10 KO fish compared to F1 NT fish (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative cell counting data with statistical analysis.

claim: At 70 days post-neocuproine treatment, MG-NT fish had regenerated an average of 82% of their melanocytes.
source: At 70 days post-neocuproine treatment, MG-NT fish had regenerated an average of 82% of their melanocytes, whereas only 53% of melanocytes had regenerated in MG-sox10 fish (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from melanocyte regeneration experiments.

claim: At 70 days post-neocuproine treatment, only 53% of melanocytes had regenerated in MG-sox10 fish.
source: At 70 days post-neocuproine treatment, MG-NT fish had regenerated an average of 82% of their melanocytes, whereas only 53% of melanocytes had regenerated in MG-sox10 fish (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from melanocyte regeneration experiments.

claim: sox10 is required for adult melanocyte regeneration.
source: These findings demonstrate that sox10 is required for adult melanocyte regeneration, highlighting its requirement within melanoblast populations outside of neural crest specification.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the regeneration experiment data.

claim: Mutation of tuba8l3a in zebrafish leads to defects in melanocyte patterning, CNS abnormalities, and altered craniofacial morphology.
source: Mutation of tubulin genes such as tuba8l3a in zebrafish leads to highly pleiotropic effects, including defects in melanocyte patterning, CNS abnormalities, and altered craniofacial morphology (Larson et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on tuba8l3a mutation phenotypes.

claim: Non-cell-type-specific knockout of tuba1a results in extensive embryo abnormalities, including a curved tail phenotype, pericardial edema, and melanocytes with more dispersed pigmentation.
source: Non-cell-type-specific knockout of tuba1a with the Alt-R CRISPR Cas9 system results in extensive embryo abnormalities, including a curved tail phenotype, pericardial edema, and melanocytes with more dispersed pigmentation (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data from Alt-R CRISPR experiments.

claim: Compared to 71% survival of NT Alt-R embryos, only 10% of embryos injected with tuba1a Alt-R survive to 14 dpf.
source: We found that compared to 71% survival of NT Alt-R embryos, only 10% of embryos injected with tuba1a Alt-R survive to 14 dpf (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative survival data from experiments.

claim: The tuba1a Alt-R guide also targets tuba1c, a gene with 99.78% homology to tuba1a in zebrafish.
source: During validation of tuba1a Alt-R, we discovered that this guide also targets tuba1c, a gene with 99.78% homology to tuba1a in zebrafish (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports sequencing data showing off-target effects.

claim: Neither tuba1a- nor tuba1c-specific guides alone were sufficient to recreate the dispersed melanocyte phenotype.
source: Despite robust cutting, neither tuba1a- nor tuba1c-specific guides alone were sufficient to recreate the dispersed melanocyte phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data testing individual guides.

claim: A second guide RNA that simultaneously targeted both tuba1a and tuba1c was able to recapitulate the dispersed melanocyte phenotype.
source: However, we were able to recapitulate our findings using a second guide RNA that simultaneously targeted both tuba1a and tuba1c, suggesting possible redundancy of these genes, with compensation masking the phenotype in single-gene knockouts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data with a dual-targeting guide.

claim: Melanocyte-specific loss of tuba1a/c resulted in viable adult fish with no obvious abnormalities.
source: Unlike global knockout of tuba1a/c, melanocyte-specific loss of tuba1a/c resulted in viable adult fish with no obvious abnormalities (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data comparing global and melanocyte-specific knockouts.

claim: No dispersed melanocyte phenotype was observed in any mitfaCas9 MG-tuba1a/c embryos.
source: Surprisingly, we did not observe the dispersed melanocyte phenotype in any mitfaCas9 MG-tuba1a/c embryos (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data from melanocyte-specific knockout experiments.

claim: tuba1a/c may be functioning in a cell non-autonomous manner on melanocytes.
source: Based on this observation, we hypothesized that tuba1a/c may be functioning in a cell non-autonomous manner on melanocytes.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this hypothesis based on the lack of phenotype in melanocyte-specific knockout.

claim: The dispersed pigmentation observed in tuba1a/c Alt-R embryos resembles that seen in blind zebrafish.
source: The dispersed pigmentation observed in tuba1a/c Alt-R embryos resembles that seen in blind zebrafish, which fail to contract their melanosomes in response to light (Neuhauss et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript compares the phenotype to a previously described phenotype in blind zebrafish.

claim: Blind zebrafish fail to contract their melanosomes in response to light.
source: The dispersed pigmentation observed in tuba1a/c Alt-R embryos resembles that seen in blind zebrafish, which fail to contract their melanosomes in response to light (Neuhauss et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on blind zebrafish phenotypes.

claim: TUBA1A mutation in humans can result in both ophthalmologic and brain abnormalities.
source: Interestingly, TUBA1A mutation in humans can result in both ophthalmologic and brain abnormalities, and morpholino-based knockdown of tuba1a in zebrafish inhibits CNS development (Myers et al., 2015; Veldman et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on human TUBA1A mutations.

claim: Morpholino-based knockdown of tuba1a in zebrafish inhibits CNS development.
source: Interestingly, TUBA1A mutation in humans can result in both ophthalmologic and brain abnormalities, and morpholino-based knockdown of tuba1a in zebrafish inhibits CNS development (Myers et al., 2015; Veldman et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on tuba1a knockdown in zebrafish.

claim: Tuba1a/c Alt-R embryos exposed to epinephrine had robust aggregation of melanosomes.
source: Tuba1a/c Alt-R embryos exposed to epinephrine had robust aggregation of melanosomes, demonstrating that the loss of tuba1a/c did not impair melanosome transport (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data from epinephrine treatment experiments.

claim: The loss of tuba1a/c did not impair melanosome transport.
source: Tuba1a/c Alt-R embryos exposed to epinephrine had robust aggregation of melanosomes, demonstrating that the loss of tuba1a/c did not impair melanosome transport (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the epinephrine experiment results.

claim: Tumor suppressors such as PTEN and TP53 are somatically inactivated in human melanoma.
source: In humans, tumor suppressors such as PTEN and TP53 are somatically inactivated in melanoma (Roh et al., 2016; Palmieri et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on tumor suppressor mutations in melanoma.

claim: The most commonly used zebrafish models of melanoma use a germline tp53 mutation.
source: In contrast, the most commonly used zebrafish models of melanoma use a germline tp53 mutation, which is not typically seen in humans with the disease and precludes our ability to discern the role of tp53 inactivation specifically in melanocytes and melanoma (Frantz and Ceol, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on zebrafish melanoma models.

claim: Global tp53 loss in zebrafish leads to a wide range of non-melanoma tumors.
source: While global tp53 loss is not lethal, it does lead to a wide range of non-melanoma tumors, which can deteriorate fish health and confound melanoma studies (Ignatius et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on tp53 loss phenotypes.

claim: Melanocyte-specific knockouts of ptena and ptenb showed an aberrant expansion of the melanocytes outside of the stripe regions they normally are restrained to.
source: We observed an aberrant expansion of the melanocytes outside of the stripe regions they normally are restrained to, suggesting that inactivation of ptena and ptenb induces defects in melanocyte patterning (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data from ptena/ptenb knockout experiments.

claim: Loss of ptena/b alone was not sufficient to induce melanoma.
source: However, loss of ptena/b alone was not sufficient to induce melanoma.
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data from tumor monitoring experiments.

claim: No tumors were detected in BFP- fish from any of the injection conditions (n=136).
source: No tumors were detected in BFP- fish from any of the injection conditions (n=136).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from tumor monitoring experiments.

claim: No tumors were observed in BFP+ fish injected with either BRAFV600E alone (n=35).
source: We also did not observe any tumors in BFP+ fish injected with either BRAFV600E alone (n=35) or ptena/b; tp53 guides in the absence of BRAFV600E (n=17).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from tumor monitoring experiments.

claim: No tumors were observed in BFP+ fish injected with ptena/b; tp53 guides in the absence of BRAFV600E (n=17).
source: We also did not observe any tumors in BFP+ fish injected with either BRAFV600E alone (n=35) or ptena/b; tp53 guides in the absence of BRAFV600E (n=17).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from tumor monitoring experiments.

claim: Approximately 5% of fish from the BRAF;tp53 group developed tumors.
source: Approximately 5% of fish from the BRAF;tp53 group developed tumors (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from tumor monitoring experiments.

claim: 6% of tp53-/- fish developed tumors when injected with a BRAFV600E construct in a previous study.
source: This aligns with a previous study where 6% of tp53-/- fish developed tumors when injected with a BRAFV600E construct (Patton et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work for comparison.

claim: Targeting of ptena and ptenb in mitfaCas9 fish co-injected with mitfa:BRAFV600E resulted in a tumor incidence of 29%.
source: Targeting of ptena and ptenb in mitfaCas9 fish co-injected with mitfa:BRAFV600E resulted in a higher tumor incidence of 29% (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from tumor monitoring experiments.

claim: When all three tumor suppressors (tp53, ptena, ptenb) were targeted in combination with BRAFV600E, 59% of fish developed tumors by 30 weeks post-fertilization (wpf).
source: When all three tumor suppressors (tp53, ptena, ptenb) were targeted in combination with BRAFV600E, 59% of fish developed tumors by 30 weeks post-fertilization (wpf) (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from tumor monitoring experiments.

claim: All tumor samples expressed BRAFV600E.
source: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) revealed that all tumor samples expressed BRAFV600E, while p-AKT, a hallmark of PTEN inactivation, was only detected in samples with ptena/b KO (Figure 5E).
evidence: The manuscript reports IHC data from tumor samples.

claim: p-AKT, a hallmark of PTEN inactivation, was only detected in tumor samples with ptena/b KO.
source: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) revealed that all tumor samples expressed BRAFV600E, while p-AKT, a hallmark of PTEN inactivation, was only detected in samples with ptena/b KO (Figure 5E).
evidence: The manuscript reports IHC data from tumor samples.

claim: A large proportion of reads contained indels at the target locus for each of the target genes (ptena, ptenb, and tp53) in tumors.
source: A large proportion of reads contained indels at the target locus for each of the target genes (ptena, ptenb, and tp53) (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports CRISPR-seq data from tumor samples.

claim: SOX10 is the top in vitro genetic dependency necessary for tumor cell proliferation according to the DepMap.
source: In melanoma, the DepMap has identified SOX10 as the top in vitro genetic dependency necessary for tumor cell proliferation, suggesting it acts as a lineage-specific oncogene (Tsherniak et al., 2017; Shakhova et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites the DepMap database and prior published work.

claim: Loss of sox10 is associated with a loss of tumor-initiating potential and cell proliferation in prior work in both zebrafish and mice.
source: In prior work in both zebrafish and mice, loss of sox10 is clearly associated with a loss of tumor-initiating potential and cell proliferation (Kaufman et al., 2016; Shakhova et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on sox10 in cancer models.

claim: sox10 inactivation markedly reduced tumor incidence in the mitfaCas9 melanoma model.
source: Consistent with the DepMap prediction, sox10 inactivation markedly reduced tumor incidence, which likely reflects loss of proliferation. Only 3/96 (3.1%) fish with sox10 knockouts initiated melanomas compared to the 24/94 fish (25.5%) from the NT condition that developed tumors (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from tumor monitoring experiments.

claim: Only 3/96 (3.1%) fish with sox10 knockouts initiated melanomas compared to 24/94 fish (25.5%) from the NT condition.
source: Consistent with the DepMap prediction, sox10 inactivation markedly reduced tumor incidence, which likely reflects loss of proliferation. Only 3/96 (3.1%) fish with sox10 knockouts initiated melanomas compared to the 24/94 fish (25.5%) from the NT condition that developed tumors (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data from tumor monitoring experiments.

claim: sox10 KO tumors expressed lower levels of Sox10 protein compared to NT tumors.
source: Using IHC, we validated that sox10 KO tumors expressed lower levels of Sox10 protein compared to NT tumors (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports IHC data from tumor samples.

claim: Two of the three sox10 KO tumors markedly upregulated sox9 relative to control tumors expressing NT gRNA.
source: To test this, we stained our sox10 CRISPR tumors for sox9 and discovered that two of the three sox10 KO tumors markedly upregulated sox9 relative to control tumors expressing NT gRNA (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports IHC data from tumor samples.

claim: In vitro, knockout of SOX10 in human melanoma cell lines is associated with acquisition of a SOX9hi state.
source: In vitro, knockout of SOX10 in a variety of human cell lines is associated with acquisition of a SOX9hi state, which has been suggested to be linked to the invasive phenotype (Wouters et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on SOX10 knockout in human cell lines.

claim: Re-analysis of publicly available RNA-seq data using three patient-derived human melanoma cell lines treated with siRNA targeting SOX10 confirmed that SOX10 knockdown lines become SOX9hi.
source: We performed a re-analysis of publicly available RNA-seq data using three patient-derived human melanoma cell lines treated with siRNA targeting SOX10 confirmed this observation, with the SOX10 lines now becoming SOX9hi (Figure 6E–J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–L; Wouters et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript reports re-analysis of published scRNA-seq data.

claim: Mitfa expression is detectable by 18 hr post-fertilization (hpf) and is highly expressed in pigment cells, including melanocytes, xanthophores, and their progenitors.
source: Mitfa expression is detectable by 18 hr post-fertilization (hpf) and is highly expressed in pigment cells, including melanocytes, xanthophores, and their progenitors.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about mitfa expression.

claim: The casper zebrafish strain harbors a premature stop codon in mitfa exon 3.
source: Furthermore, targeting Cas9 to exon 2 offers the flexibility of replicating this knock-in strategy in casper zebrafish, a transparent fish widely used for melanoma studies that harbor a premature stop codon in mitfa exon 3 (White et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on the casper strain.

claim: Zebrafish have four dark stripes occupied by melanocytes, which alternate with light-colored interstripes occupied by yellow-pigmented xanthophores.
source: Zebrafish have four dark stripes occupied by melanocytes, which alternate with light-colored interstripes occupied by yellow-pigmented xanthophores (Owen et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on zebrafish pigment patterning.

claim: Melanocytes continually regenerate throughout life, typically from a progenitor population of melanoblasts or melanocyte stem cells.
source: Melanocytes continually regenerate throughout life, typically from a progenitor population of melanoblasts or melanocyte stem cells.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about melanocyte biology.

claim: Neocuproine is a copper chelator previously shown to kill mature, pigmented melanocytes.
source: We treated adult fish with neocuproine, a copper chelator previously shown to kill mature, pigmented melanocytes (O'Reilly-Pol and Johnson, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on neocuproine effects.

claim: Microtubules are critical for the transport of melanosomes in melanocytic cells.
source: Microtubules are also critical for the transport of melanosomes in melanocytic cells (Rogers et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on melanosome transport.

claim: Germline knockout of ptena/b is embryonic lethal in zebrafish.
source: Like sox10 and tuba1a/c, germline knockout of ptena/b is embryonic lethal (Croushore et al., 2005; Faucherre et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on ptena/b knockout phenotypes.

claim: In ptena/ptenb F0 melanocyte-specific KO fish, survival was normal.
source: In our ptena/ptenb F0 melanocyte-specific KO fish, survival was normal.
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data from melanocyte-specific knockout experiments.

claim: Expression of BRAFV600E and loss of tp53 in WT (non-casper) fish results in relatively low tumor burden.
source: Previous studies have shown that expression of BRAFV600E and loss of tp53 in WT (non-casper) fish results in relatively low tumor burden, suggesting that the casper strain might be especially tumor prone in the setting of MiniCoopR mitfa rescue, although the exact reasons for this are not clear.
evidence: The manuscript references prior studies without specific citations.

claim: Ptena/ptenb loss in combination with tp53 has been shown to accelerate melanoma formation in zebrafish.
source: Ptena/ptenb loss in combination with tp53 has been shown to accelerate melanoma formation in zebrafish (He et al., 2021; Montal et al., 2024).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on ptena/ptenb and tp53 in melanoma.

claim: In melanoma, the proliferative state is thought to be characterized by high expression of SOX10.
source: In melanoma, the proliferative state is thought to be characterized by high expression of SOX10, whereas the mesenchymal, invasive state is characterized by high expression of SOX9 (Wouters et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on melanoma cell states.

claim: The mesenchymal, invasive state in melanoma is characterized by high expression of SOX9.
source: In melanoma, the proliferative state is thought to be characterized by high expression of SOX10, whereas the mesenchymal, invasive state is characterized by high expression of SOX9 (Wouters et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on melanoma cell states.

claim: The mitfaCas9 system allows for specific gene disruption across the melanocyte developmental lineage.
source: By integrating the Cas9 nuclease into the endogenous melanocyte-specific mitfa locus, we achieved specific gene disruption across the melanocyte developmental lineage.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: The mitfaCas9 system can be used to inactivate genes in melanocytes without additional developmental or off-target phenotypes.
source: We used our mitfaCas9 knock-in animals to inactivate the pigmentation gene albino and the embryonic essential genes sox10, tuba1a, and ptena/b in melanocytes without additional developmental or off-target phenotypes.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from multiple experiments.

claim: The mitfaCas9 system can be used to induce melanomas in wild-type fish by inactivating tumor suppressors tp53 and ptena/b within melanocytes that also express BRAFV600E.
source: We also demonstrated that this system can be used to induce melanomas in wild-type (WT) fish by inactivating the tumor suppressors tp53 and ptena/b within melanocytes that also express the melanoma oncogene BRAFV600E.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from melanoma experiments.

claim: Inactivating sox10 in BRAFV600E melanomas significantly decreased melanoma initiation.
source: Inactivating the neural crest transcription factor sox10 in these tumors significantly decreased melanoma initiation but resulted in rare invasive tumors that highly expressed the sox9 transcription factor, highlighting that unexpected in vivo phenotypes can emerge that aren't predicted from in vitro studies (Capparelli et al., 2022; Wouters et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from sox10 knockout melanoma experiments.

claim: Inactivating sox10 in BRAFV600E melanomas resulted in rare invasive tumors that highly expressed sox9.
source: Inactivating the neural crest transcription factor sox10 in these tumors significantly decreased melanoma initiation but resulted in rare invasive tumors that highly expressed the sox9 transcription factor, highlighting that unexpected in vivo phenotypes can emerge that aren't predicted from in vitro studies (Capparelli et al., 2022; Wouters et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from sox10 knockout melanoma experiments.

claim: Unexpected in vivo phenotypes can emerge that aren't predicted from in vitro studies.
source: Inactivating the neural crest transcription factor sox10 in these tumors significantly decreased melanoma initiation but resulted in rare invasive tumors that highly expressed the sox9 transcription factor, highlighting that unexpected in vivo phenotypes can emerge that aren't predicted from in vitro studies (Capparelli et al., 2022; Wouters et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript draws this general conclusion from the sox10 experiments and cites related work.

claim: The MAZERATI system uses tissue-specific promoter transgenes to drive Cas9 expression, which are introduced via plasmid injection into one-cell stage embryos.
source: For example, the MAZERATI system uses tissue-specific promoter transgenes to drive Cas9 expression, which are introduced via plasmid injection into one-cell stage embryos (Ablain et al., 2015; Ablain et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on the MAZERATI system.

claim: Promoter fragment transgenes could lack certain regulatory regions.
source: One potential limitation of promoter fragment transgenes is that these fragments could lack certain regulatory regions.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about a potential limitation of promoter-based systems.

claim: The mitfa-Cas9 knock-in line maintains the endogenous regulatory elements needed for control of the mitfa gene.
source: One difference between our mitfa-Cas9 knock-in line compared to MAZERATI is that it maintains the endogenous regulatory elements needed for control of the mitfa gene.
evidence: The manuscript describes a key feature of their system.

claim: MITF transcription acts as a 'rheostat' in melanoma.
source: We do not yet fully know when or if this difference would be important, but given the complex role of MITF transcription as a 'rheostat' in melanoma (Hoek and Goding, 2010), it is reasonable to assume these endogenous elements could become important in some circumstances.
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on MITF function in melanoma.

claim: SOX9 is increasingly recognized to be a potent mediator of tumor cell invasiveness.
source: SOX9 is increasingly recognized to be a potent mediator of tumor cell invasiveness, so it is possible this could explain the somewhat more mesenchymal/invasive appearance of these tumors (Cheng et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on SOX9 function in cancer.

claim: A similar phenomenon of transcription factor switching has been observed for MITF in melanoma.
source: Whether this phenomenon of SOX10/SOX9 switching is a general phenomenon, or specific to that class of TFs, remains to be determined. However, a similar phenomenon has been observed for MITF, another melanocytic TF, suggesting this idea of TF switching needs to be more thoroughly explored in the future (Hoek et al., 2008; Hossain and Eccles, 2023; Travnickova et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on MITF switching in melanoma.
